title: EF Core vs Dapper vs Raw SQL
description: Learn to choose the right data access strategy in C# by understanding the trade-offs between EF Core's productivity, Dapper's performance, and raw SQL's control.

data.text: Every C# application must read and write data, and the choice of data access library is one of the most consequential architecture decisions. EF Core offers productivity, change tracking, and LINQ queries. Dapper offers raw performance and explicit SQL control. Raw ADO.NET offers maximum control but maximum boilerplate. None is universally best. The senior engineer chooses the tool based on the query complexity, performance requirements, and team expertise.

A common mistake is using EF Core for every query because it is the default in new projects. EF Core is excellent for domain modeling, change tracking, and standard CRUD operations. But for high-throughput read paths, complex reporting queries, or bulk operations, EF Core's abstraction can become a performance bottleneck. Dapper or raw SQL are not regressions; they are deliberate choices that match the tool to the workload.

cards.title: EF Core
cards.description: Full-featured ORM with LINQ, migrations, and change tracking.
cons: Query performance can lag raw SQL

cards.title: Dapper
cards.description: Micro-ORM that maps SQL results to objects with minimal overhead.
cons: Less protection from SQL injection if careless

cards.title: Raw ADO.NET
cards.description: Direct use of SqlConnection, SqlCommand, and data readers.
pros: Full access to SQL Server features

data.title: When to use each data access strategy
items: Use EF Core when the domain is complex, change tracking is valuable, or the team prioritizes development speed over raw query performance.
Use Dapper when queries are performance-critical, the SQL is complex or hand-tuned, or you need multi-mapping for stored procedures.
Use raw ADO.NET only for extreme edge cases: bulk operations, streaming large datasets, or when Dapper's abstraction is still too heavy.

data.title: Hybrid approach is common and recommended
data.text: Many production C# applications use EF Core for most data access and Dapper for specific hot paths. This is not a compromise; it is a deliberate optimization. EF Core handles the domain model, while Dapper handles the high-throughput queries that need every millisecond of performance.

data.text: Dapper executes raw SQL and maps the results to objects. The SQL is explicit, which means you can see exactly what hits the database and optimize it directly.

data.text: EF Core has improved dramatically in recent versions, but it still generates SQL that is not always optimal. The N+1 query problem, where a loop triggers a database call per item, is the most common performance pitfall. Dapper eliminates this by giving you full control over the SQL. If you use EF Core, always profile the generated SQL with logging or a tool like MiniProfiler to ensure it matches your expectations.

data.title: Profile and optimize a data access query
data.description: Take an existing EF Core query and evaluate whether Dapper or raw SQL would be more appropriate.
steps: Find a data access method in your project that uses EF Core.
Enable SQL logging and capture the generated SQL for a representative request.
Analyze the SQL for N+1 queries, unnecessary joins, or missing indexes.
Rewrite the same query using Dapper with explicit SQL.
Compare the execution plans and measure the performance difference.
Decide whether to keep EF Core, switch to Dapper, or split: EF Core for simple paths, Dapper for the hot path.
data.expectedOutcome: A side-by-side comparison of EF Core and Dapper for the same query, with a justified recommendation.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: EF Core is best for domain-heavy code where productivity and change tracking matter.
Dapper is best for high-throughput, complex queries where SQL control and performance matter.
Raw ADO.NET is rarely needed; Dapper covers almost every case where EF Core is too slow.
The hybrid approach is common and recommended: EF Core for the domain, Dapper for hot paths.
data.takeaway: Data access is not a one-size-fits-all decision. Senior engineers match the tool to the workload, using the right library for each bounded context and query pattern.
